title: Gigot d'Agneau
subtitle: Roast leg of lamb with garlic and rosemary
excerpt: A whole leg of lamb spiked with garlic cloves and rosemary, roasted until pink at the centre. The French tradition is to serve lamb considerably pinker than British convention, this recipe gives both options.
sourceNotes: Gigot d'agneau is one of the great Sunday roasts of French cooking. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), is explicit that the French serve their roast lamb far pinker than British convention would permit, giving a recommended internal temperature of 65°C for the centre. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives a detailed method. The dish is associated with Easter Sunday across Catholic France.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The lamb can be spiked with garlic and rosemary and returned to the fridge up to 24 hours before roasting. Remove from the fridge 45 minutes before roasting.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving cooked meat covered loosely with foil before carving, so the juices redistribute through the fibres as the muscle relaxes. Resting is especially important for a large roast like a leg of lamb; without it, the juices run out when the meat is cut and the slices are drier.

content.text: Gigot d'agneau is a whole leg of lamb spiked with slivers of garlic and sprigs of rosemary and roasted in a hot oven. The French tradition is to serve it considerably pinker than British convention allows, the internal temperature at the thickest point is 60°C to 65°C rather than 70°C to 75°C. Both approaches are given in the instructions below; the final choice is yours.
An instant-read thermometer is essential for a roast this size. Resting is equally important: a leg of lamb that is carved immediately loses its juices to the board.

items.prepNote: bone-in, about 2 kg, at room temperature

content.text: Use a small knife to make 24 deep cuts over the surface of the lamb leg, each about 2 cm deep. Push a sliver of garlic and a small piece of rosemary into each cut. Rub the lamb all over with olive oil and season generously with salt and pepper. Allow to come fully to room temperature before roasting, at least 45 minutes out of the fridge.
Heat the oven to 220°C fan. Place the lamb in the roasting tin and roast at 220°C for 20 minutes to brown the outside.

Reduce the oven to 180°C fan and continue to roast. Timing guide from this point: 12 to 14 minutes per 500 g for pink (internal temperature 60°C to 65°C); 15 to 18 minutes per 500 g for just-cooked-through (70°C to 73°C). For a 2 kg leg, this means a total oven time of approximately 60 to 75 minutes after the initial blast.

Check with the instant-read thermometer, inserting at the thickest part away from the bone. When the target temperature is reached, transfer to a warm plate, cover loosely with foil, and rest for 20 minutes before carving.
The resting period is not optional. A large joint that is not rested will lose its juices when carved.
Cover the lamb loosely with foil and a clean tea towel to retain heat.

items.symptom: The outside is browning faster than expected
items.cause: The oven runs hot, or the lamb was placed too high in the oven.
items.fix: Cover loosely with foil and move to a lower shelf. The outside needs to be sealed but not burnt.

items.symptom: The thermometer reads lower than expected after the calculated time
items.cause: The lamb was cold when it went into the oven, or the joint was larger than the calculation assumed.
items.fix: Return to the oven and continue checking every 10 minutes. Never rely solely on timing, a thermometer gives the only reliable reading.

items.symptom: The lamb is very rare in the centre near the bone
items.cause: The bone conducts heat slowly, so the meat near the bone is always the coolest. The thermometer must be inserted away from the bone.
items.fix: Return to the oven for 10 more minutes. Measure the temperature in the thickest part of the muscle, not adjacent to the bone.

items.symptom: The juices have all run out when carving
items.cause: The lamb was not rested, or was carved before the rest period was complete.
items.fix: Rest for a minimum of 20 minutes, covered. The juices in the roasting tin (after skimming the fat) make an immediate simple sauce.

content.text: Roast lamb is the Easter dish of France. It is as closely tied to the spring festival in France as it is to the British Sunday lunch. The lamb from the salt-meadow pastures of the Vendée, Brittany, and Normandy (agneau de pré-salé) is especially prized. The animals graze on salt-marsh grasses, which give the meat a natural seasoning and a particular flavour. French lamb is typically sold younger than British lamb. A leg of one to two years produces a leaner, more delicate result than the older animals more common in Britain.
